name: Caffeine avoidance

card.summary: Dropping caffeine to reduce puffiness and improve sleep; sleep effects are documented, puffiness is untested.
card.note: Withdrawal headaches are common for a day or so.

quick.overview:
Some people avoid caffeine hoping for a less puffy face and better sleep.

Caffeine can disrupt sleep, but no study links avoiding it to reduced facial puffiness.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, promoting wakefulness and a brief diuretic effect in non-habitual users.
quick.risks: Quitting can cause withdrawal symptoms such as headache and fatigue for a short time.

lead: Caffeine avoidance is the practice of cutting out coffee, tea, energy drinks and other caffeinated products. In appearance-focused communities it is usually pursued to improve sleep and, by extension, how rested and un-puffy the face looks the next day, and sometimes to reduce jitteriness or skin flare-ups that people attribute to stimulants.[1]

Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant that can delay or prevent sleep and lengthen the time taken to fall asleep; Wikipedia reports that even about 100 mg a day can disrupt sleep in some people, while others show little effect, and that its half-life in healthy adults is about 3 to 7 hours.[1] Sleep is the link practitioners rely on for appearance: Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness lists interrupted sleep among common causes of puffy eyes, along with dietary sodium, alcohol, allergies and fluid retention.[3] That article does not name caffeine as a cause.

Large acute doses (roughly 250 to 300 mg or more) increase urine output, but mainly in people who have gone days or weeks without caffeine; regular users develop tolerance.[1] No published study has tested caffeine avoidance as a way to reduce facial puffiness or improve skin.

chain: Sleep is easier to start and keep (for people sensitive to caffeine)
Better rested, less puffy look the next morning
angle.text: People who avoid caffeine do so to protect sleep and avoid stimulant effects, aiming for a fresher, less puffy-looking face. The link runs through sleep quality, which varies widely between individuals in how much caffeine affects it.

infobox: 400 mg/day for healthy adults (EFSA, Health Canada)[1]

sections.h: Effects relevant to the appearance aim
paras: Wikipedia reports that around 100 mg a day may disrupt sleep in some regular users, though many develop tolerance to caffeine's effects on blood pressure, heart rate and alertness with regular use.[1]
The diuretic effect appears in people who have abstained and fades with regular intake, so the fluid-loss effect is limited mainly to acute large doses in non-habitual users.[1]

Mild physical dependence can occur with more than 100 mg a day. Withdrawal is self-reported by about 11 percent of users, though only about half of those show it in laboratory testing, and it typically lasts no more than a day at lower intakes.[1] Symptoms listed under DSM-5 criteria include fatigue, headache, irritability and trouble concentrating.[1] A 2026 study examined acute caffeine withdrawal and headache among regular coffee drinkers.[5]

EFSA states that up to 400 mg a day is not a safety concern for healthy adults, and Health Canada advises the same ceiling; for pregnancy and breastfeeding EFSA sets 200 mg and Health Canada 300 mg.[1] The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding caffeine under age 18.[1]
A 2017 umbrella review summarised on Wikipedia found coffee generally safe at usual intakes.[2]

Members of appearance communities link caffeine to puffiness and poor sleep and may swap it for decaffeinated or herbal drinks. Alongside it, people commonly adjust salt and alcohol, which are also cited as causes of facial puffiness.[3]

No studies found on caffeine avoidance and facial puffiness. Related research includes a review of whether caffeine should be avoided after free-flap surgery and Cochrane reviews of restricted maternal caffeine intake in pregnancy, which address different outcomes.[4][6]
